title: Temporal Decomposition
pattern: The system structure is organized to match the chronological order of execution steps (first read, then parse), forcing multiple modules to deal with the same underlying raw data representation.
why_bad: It causes information leakage. The chronological stages are forced to share knowledge about the exact same data format or protocol. If the format changes, multiple sequentially-decomposed classes/structs must change together, breaking encapsulation.
detection: Distinct structs or modules named after sequential execution phases (e.g., `Reader` -> `Parser` -> `Writer`) that pass raw, un-abstracted representation formats (like raw strings, raw buffers) from one to the next.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Standardized compilers or multi-stage pipelines where intermediate representations (like ASTs or bytecode) are explicitly typed and stable.
fix: Combine the chronological steps that share the same representation details into a single, cohesive module that hides these details from the rest of the application.
source: John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 5 ("Information Hiding - Temporal Decomposition"), pp. 32, 302–303.
